title: Gold Rebounds Above $4,300 as Dollar Eases and Investors Digest Fed Hike
excerpt: Spot bullion rose more than 1% to $4,310 an ounce on Thursday, bouncing off a near six-week low as easing oil prices and a softer dollar offset the Fed's hawkish rate increase.
body:
• Spot gold climbed more than 1% to $4,310 an ounce on Thursday, recovering from a near six-week low hit the day of the Fed's rate hike.
  • The bounce was driven by an easing dollar, falling oil prices, and technical buying — with the Fed's hawkish message already priced in.
  • Silver led the metals rally, while a pullback in Treasury yields from multi-year highs reduced the opportunity cost of holding bullion.
  • Analysts caution the recovery is fragile: gold remains range-bound until the Fed's next moves and the oil price path become clearer.

Gold prices climbed more than 1% on Thursday as investors digested the Federal Reserve's interest-rate hike and an easing in the oil rally, with spot bullion reclaiming ground above $4,300 an ounce after touching a near six-week low the previous session.

Spot gold was up 1.1% at $4,310.49 per ounce, according to Reuters, offsetting a 0.7% overnight fall. US gold futures for December delivery traded around $4,348.70. The move marked a sharp reversal of sentiment: just a day earlier, gold had been pinned near $4,288 as traders braced for the Fed's widely expected quarter-point increase to 3.75%-4%.

Higher rates are normally bad news for gold. Bullion pays no yield, so each rate increase raises the opportunity cost of holding it. But with markets having priced a 92% probability of the hike, according to CME FedWatch, the actual decision removed a layer of uncertainty rather than adding a new shock.

What drove the rebound

Three forces lined up behind the metal. First, oil prices slipped, extending overnight losses as reports of Saudi Arabia offering extra crude cargoes through Oman eased fears of supply disruption from the Middle East conflict. Brent crude fell about 0.7% to $105.05 a barrel after dropping 2.7% the previous day. Lower oil prices reduce the inflation impulse that the Fed is fighting — and paradoxically, they also remove one of the pressures weighing on gold.

Second, the dollar softened. The greenback had surged to a seven-week high of 100.33 against its major peers in the hours after the Fed decision, lifted by two-year Treasury yields spiking to their highest since July 2024. By Thursday the currency was easing, making dollar-priced gold cheaper for overseas buyers.

Third, Treasury yields pulled back from multi-year highs. The 10-year yield had hit 5% on Monday for the first time since October 2023, but eased to around 4.99% after the Fed meeting — a move that ING's Padhraic Garvey read as the market nodding approval at "the hike as an inflation containment one."

The technical picture

Analysts describe much of Thursday's move as technical. FXStreet noted that gold had been holding a key "neckline" near $4,333 into the decision and bounced about $50 overnight, with silver — up more than gold — leading the charge. Silver steadied near $63.67 an ounce, its fourth sharp move in eight sessions.

The caution in the commentary was plain. "Oil prices remain a key factor to watch. If oil prices continue to decline, that could support gold prices moving higher, at least from a medium-term perspective. Until that materializes, I expect gold to remain range-bound," Kelvin Wong, senior market analyst at OANDA, told Reuters.

IG market analyst Tony Sycamore had flagged before the decision that what mattered most for gold was not the hike itself but how Chairman Kevin Warsh framed it: "If he casts it as the start of a meeting-by-meeting tightening cycle, that would be a hit to gold and to risk assets overall. If instead he signals a preference for a more measured pace, that would prove somewhat supportive for risk sentiment and for gold." Warsh landed closer to the measured end, with officials projecting just two hikes this year and none in 2027.

"Oil prices remain a key factor to watch. If oil prices continue to decline, that could support gold prices moving higher, at least from a medium-term perspective."

— Kelvin Wong, Senior Market Analyst, OANDA

Gold's deeper bid

Beyond the day's trading, gold's resilience has surprised even seasoned observers. Commerzbank noted it was "somewhat surprising" that prices had not come under greater pressure, pointing to persistent fiscal concerns — US government debt has topped $40 trillion — and elevated long-term bond yields as structural supports.

ANZ's Daniel Hynes made the same point: gold is supported "as US fiscal pressures continue to undermine confidence in the long-term value of government debt and the currency used to finance it."

What it means for investors and buyers

The metal sits at the intersection of two big trades. As an inflation hedge, it benefits from the Middle East conflict and sticky price pressures. As a non-yielding asset, it suffers every time the Fed turns hawkish. With 16 of 18 Fed policymakers now expecting at least one more hike by year's end, the second force has not gone away.

For Indian households — among the world's largest holders of gold — the bounce above $4,300 extends a remarkable run. Gold has traded near record territory for most of 2026, and every dollar of the rebound adds directly to the value of jewelry and savings held in homes across the diaspora and the subcontinent.

What to watch next

Traders now look to Friday's US inflation data and the Bank of England's Thursday decision for the next directional cue. If oil keeps sliding and the dollar stays soft, gold's fragile recovery could build. If inflation surprises to the upside and the Fed's second hike gets pulled forward, the near-six-week low it just escaped may be tested again.
